title: Harborcoat
description: The explosive opening track of Reckoning, seen here in its segment of Left of Reckoning — James Herbert's surreal 1984 short film shot among the whirligigs at R.A. Miller's farm in Rabbittown, Georgia.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Reckoning, R.E.M.'s second album, released April 9, 1984 on I.R.S. Records.
It kicks off with a quick Bill Berry drum roll and bright, ringing Peter Buck guitar chords — the band announcing a rawer sound than Murmur.
Reckoning was produced by Don Dixon and Mitch Easter, the same team behind Murmur, at Reflection Sound Studios in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Like every early R.E.M. song, it's credited to all four members: Berry, Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe.
Hear Mills singing counterpoint behind Stipe? Mills wrote his own backing-vocal words — he later confirmed it on Twitter.
Stipe's lyric is famously opaque, opening with 'They crowded up to Lenin with their noses worn off.'
Mid-song Stipe spells out the aside 'R-E-A-C-T' after the line about a splinter in your eye that 'reads react.'
This footage is from Left of Reckoning, the short film Stipe commissioned to accompany the album's first side, directed by Athens filmmaker James Herbert.
Herbert filmed it in March 1984 at folk artist R.A. Miller's Whirligig Farm in Rabbittown, Georgia — those spinning sculptures fill the frame.
Segments of Left of Reckoning aired on MTV, making this arty film clip the closest thing 'Harborcoat' ever had to a conventional music video.

title: Little T&A
description: Keith Richards' cheerfully shameless Tattoo You rocker — his traditional lead-vocal slot on the album, built from an Emotional Rescue-era outtake and presented here in its official remastered audio video.

pops.text: This is Keith Richards' lead-vocal turn on Tattoo You (1981) — every Stones album reserved him at least one song out front.
Its working title was 'Bulldog,' and it was credited, as usual, to Jagger/Richards, though it's largely Keith's composition.
Richards began it in early 1979 for Emotional Rescue, left it off that album, then reworked it in mid-1981 for Tattoo You.
Tattoo You itself was stitched together mostly from outtakes, because the band needed a new album to tour behind in 1981.
Keith doesn't just sing: he plays lead and rhythm guitar AND the bass on this track.
That's Ronnie Wood on guitar alongside him, Charlie Watts on drums, and founding sixth Stone Ian Stewart on piano.
Mick Jagger stays in the background here, adding backing vocals to Keith's lead.
Richards admitted the song was proudly lowbrow, calling the finished mix 'nice and dumb, which is what it's supposed to be.'
The Stones played it throughout their 1981 American tour, then revived it on the 2006 A Bigger Bang tour — a performance appears on the Shine a Light soundtrack.
The track got a second life on the soundtrack of Argo, the 2012 film that won the Academy Award for Best Picture.

title: Calls That Never Connected
description: A 2026 blues single from the prolific promptgenix catalog — no performance video exists, so this is the official DistroKid-provided YouTube audio release that accompanied the single.

pops.text: This was released as a standalone single on February 23, 2026, by 10302836 Records DK.
Shazam and Apple Music classify promptgenix under Blues — this track sits in that blues and rock-blues lane.
The songwriting credit listed by Shazam goes to C T C, with promptgenix credited as producer.
This YouTube version was provided directly by DistroKid, the distributor behind the release — it's an auto-generated audio video, not a filmed performance.
There is no official music video for the song; the single's artwork is the whole visual.
promptgenix released music at a remarkable pace in 2026, with album series including Digital Delta and Underworld Blues appearing the same year.
This single arrived just two weeks after 'They'll Call This an Accident,' released February 9, 2026 on Digital Delta: volume four.
The song found an audience on TikTok, where fan edits tagged it #rockmusic and #blues and framed it as a song about missed calls and people who never answer.
On South Africa's Apple Music blues chart in late October 2026, the track was still sitting at #4 — with another promptgenix song at #1.
On Last.fm the track is promptgenix's top-listed song, a small but telling footprint for a word-of-mouth digital release.

title: Travelin' Light
description: Widespread Panic's swaggering take on J.J. Cale's song, performed live on Late Night with Conan O'Brien on August 4, 1998 by the band's classic lineup — the version of record from their 1998 live album Light Fuse, Get Away.

pops.text: First, the songwriter: this is a J.J. Cale song. Cale first released it on his 1976 album Troubadour.
Cale was the Tulsa songwriter whose 'After Midnight' and 'Cocaine' became hits for Eric Clapton — Panic were covering a master.
Panic had played 'Travelin' Light' since their early days; it was a live staple long before it appeared on a record.
This performance comes from Late Night with Conan O'Brien, August 4, 1998 — one of the band's first three appearances on the show, later shared on Panic's own YouTube channel.
That's the classic lineup: John Bell and Michael Houser on guitars, Dave Schools on bass, John 'JoJo' Hermann on keys, Todd Nance on drums and Domingo 'Sunny' Ortiz on percussion.
Guitarist Michael Houser, whose swirling lead style defined the band's sound, died in 2002 — footage like this is the original Panic at full strength.
The band's released version appears on Light Fuse, Get Away, their 1998 live album.
That live album was produced and mixed by John Keane, the Athens producer who worked with the band throughout their career.
Panic formed in Athens, Georgia, in 1986 — the same college-town scene that produced R.E.M. and the B-52's.
Decades on, the song is still in the band's live rotation — it turns up in Panic setlists from Red Rocks to New Orleans Jazz Fest.

title: Bertha
description: A Grateful Dead show-opener for the ages: 'Bertha' kicking off New Year's Eve 1987 at the Oakland Coliseum, from the band's official All the Years Live archive series. The song itself debuted on record as the opener of 1971's Skull & Roses.

pops.text: Jerry Garcia wrote the music and Robert Hunter the words — one of their defining songwriting partnerships.
The song first appeared in 1971 as the opening track of the live album Grateful Dead, better known as Skull & Roses, recorded at the Fillmore East on April 27, 1971.
Remarkably, the Dead never recorded a studio version — archivist David Lemieux notes the Skull & Roses live take is the definitive one.
It stayed in the repertoire constantly from 1971 right through 1995, the band's final year.
This performance opens the New Year's Eve 1987 show at the Oakland Coliseum — 'Bertha' was a classic first-song cannonball.
That 1987 show was broadcast live as a pay-per-view event and later released on VHS in 1996 as Ticket to New Year's.
On keyboards here is Brent Mydland, the Dead's keyboardist from 1979 until his death in 1990.
The famous fan story — that the song was named after a dangerous office fan called Bertha — is backwards: Hunter said the fan was named after the song.
Hunter described 'Bertha' itself in vaguer terms, as a connotation of birth, death and reincarnation.
This clip comes from All the Years Live, the official archive video series curated by Dead legacy manager David Lemieux.

title: Welcome To New York
description: The synth-pop opening track of 1989, Taylor's love letter to her new hometown — presented here in the official lyric video for the 2023 Taylor's Version re-recording.

pops.text: This is the opening track of 1989 (2014), the album that completed Swift's move from country to full pop.
She co-wrote it with OneRepublic frontman Ryan Tedder, who co-produced it with Noel Zancanella and Swift.
It was inspired by her real life: Swift relocated to New York City in April 2014, months before the album arrived.
Swift said she put it first because New York had become 'an important landscape and location for the story of my life.'
It was released on October 20, 2014 as a promotional single, one week ahead of the album — fans who pre-ordered got it instantly.
The original version peaked at #19 on the Billboard Hot 100.
New York took the hint: in 2014 Swift was named the city's Global Welcome Ambassador for tourism.
The bridge's line about how 'you can want who you want — boys and boys and girls and girls' was widely noted as a welcome-home message to the city's LGBTQ community.
After the dispute over her master recordings, she re-recorded the song for 1989 (Taylor's Version), released October 27, 2023 — nine years to the day after the original album.
This lyric video is for that Taylor's Version, which reached #14 on the Hot 100 — nearly matching the original's peak, a decade later.

title: Modern Love
description: Bowie's gospel-tinged Let's Dance opener in its official video — director Jim Yukich's film of the Serious Moonlight tour performing live in Philadelphia in July 1983.

pops.text: This opens Let's Dance (1983), the album that made Bowie a full-blown pop superstar in America.
It was co-produced by Bowie and Chic's Nile Rodgers, who rebuilt Bowie's sound around dancefloor grooves.
That's a young Stevie Ray Vaughan playing lead guitar — Bowie recruited him after seeing him at the Montreux Jazz Festival.
Released as a single in September 1983, it reached #2 in the UK and #14 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The video, directed by Jim Yukich, isn't a studio shoot: it's Bowie performing the song live in Philadelphia on July 20, 1983, on the Serious Moonlight tour.
The call-and-response structure — 'Modern love walks beside me' answered by the band — borrows straight from gospel and Little Richard, a stated influence on the song.
Its lyric sets faith against modern life: 'I never want to fall for modern love,' yet he puts his trust 'in God and man.'
Let's Dance was recorded at the Power Station in New York in late 1982, in sessions that took barely three weeks.
In 1987 Bowie re-recorded the song as a duet with Tina Turner for a Pepsi commercial, playing a scientist who creates her character.
A new generation met the song through Frances Ha (2012), where Greta Gerwig's character runs and dances through New York streets to it.

title: Disappear
description: The second single from X, INXS's follow-up to Kick — Michael Hutchence and the band riding through a Japanese fairground as it is built and dismantled around them, in the official remastered video.

pops.text: This was the second single from X (1990), the Australian band's follow-up to their blockbuster album Kick.
It was written by keyboardist/guitarist Jon Farriss and singer Michael Hutchence.
Released in late 1990, it climbed to #8 on the Billboard Hot 100 — bigger in America than at home, where it reached #23 in Australia.
It also hit #6 on the US Mainstream Rock chart and #10 on the alternative chart, and #21 in the UK.
It proved to be INXS's last Top 10 single in the United States.
X was produced by Chris Thomas, who had also produced Kick — the band deliberately kept the winning team together.
The video puts the band on rides at a fairground in Japan, filmed as the fair is set up and then taken down around them.
The Farriss brothers — Jon, Andrew and Tim — formed the band's core, having played together since school in Sydney.
Hutchence's vocal rides a lyric about a lover who makes the rest of the world 'disappear' — escapism as a love song.
The band performed the song at Wembley Stadium on July 13, 1991, the concert later released as Live Baby Live.

title: When the Levee Breaks
description: Led Zeppelin IV's thunderous closing track in its official audio video — a 1929 Memphis Minnie blues rebuilt around John Bonham's stairwell-recorded drums, the most sampled drum break in rock.

pops.text: This closes the band's untitled fourth album — Led Zeppelin IV — released November 8, 1971.
It's a reworking of a 1929 country-blues song by Kansas Joe McCoy and Memphis Minnie, about the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927.
The writing credit reflects that: Memphis Minnie shares it with all four members of Led Zeppelin.
That opening drum sound was recorded at Headley Grange, a Hampshire country house, with Bonham's kit set up in the entrance-hall stairwell.
Engineer Andy Johns hung two Beyerdynamic M160 microphones up the stairwell and ran them through compression and a Binson Echorec echo unit.
Bonham was playing a brand-new drum kit, which engineers credited partly for the sound's extra brightness and power.
Robert Plant's harmonica was treated with reverse echo — the echo arrives just before the note itself, creating that haunted swell.
The song was never released as a single, and Zeppelin struggled to reproduce it on stage — they only played it on the opening dates of their 1975 US tour.
That two-bar drum break became one of the most sampled sounds in music, used by the Beastie Boys, Eminem, Björk and Beyoncé, among many others.
Bonham's son Jason called this intro 'the drum intro of the Gods' — play it anywhere, he said, and people know it's John Bonham.

title: Message In A Bottle
description: The Police's first UK #1 — Sting's castaway anthem in its official video, a loose dressing-room performance with Stewart Copeland drumming on the back of a chair.

pops.text: This was the lead single from the Police's second album, Reggatta de Blanc (1979) — a made-up French-ish title meaning 'white reggae.'
Sting wrote it alone: a castaway sends out an SOS in a bottle, then discovers a hundred billion bottles washed up on the shore.
Released in September 1979, it became the first of the band's five UK #1 singles.
In America it was a slow burn at first, peaking at only #74 on the Hot 100 — the band's US breakthrough came later.
It was recorded at Surrey Sound Studios in Leatherhead, produced by Nigel Gray with the band.
Andy Summers turned Sting's simple riff into that famous rolling, arpeggiated guitar figure that drives the whole record.
The band had already road-tested it: its live debut came at Hatfield Polytechnic on February 21, 1979, filmed for the BBC's Rock Goes to College.
The cheap-and-cheerful video was shot in a theatre dressing room — Copeland drums on the back of a chair, a running gag in early Police clips.
Sting later reworked its theme in reverse: 'Fortress Around Your Heart' (1985) answers this song's plea from inside the walls.
When the Police reunited for their 2007–08 world tour, this was a centerpiece of what became one of the highest-grossing tours of its era.

title: Mary Jane's Last Dance
description: Petty's macabre MTV classic: he plays a morgue assistant who takes Kim Basinger home for one last dance, in Keir McFarlane's video that won Best Male Video at the 1994 MTV Video Music Awards.

pops.text: Petty started this song during the Full Moon Fever sessions — he had the verses for years before the chorus existed.
Producer Rick Rubin heard the unfinished tape and pushed him to finish it; Petty wrote the chorus while working on Wildflowers.
The original chorus was completely different: 'Hey, Indiana Girl, go out and find the world' — a nod to the lyric's Indiana town.
It was finally completed as one of two new songs recorded for the band's 1993 Greatest Hits album.
It became a hit in its own right: #14 on the Billboard Hot 100 and #1 on the Mainstream Rock chart.
It was also the last Heartbreakers recording with original drummer Stan Lynch, who left the band in 1994.
The video, directed by Keir McFarlane, casts Petty as a mortician's assistant infatuated with a beautiful corpse.
The corpse is played by Kim Basinger — she stays limp through a dinner date and a dance in a wedding dress.
Petty finally carries her to the ocean and lets her go; as she sinks, her eyes open. The video won Best Male Video at the 1994 MTV VMAs.
Petty himself was ambivalent for years, saying he complained about the song constantly while making it — then was glad he did.

title: Computer Blue
description: Purple Rain's frantic funk-rock centerpiece as performed in the film itself — Prince and the Revolution tearing through it at First Avenue, the performance scene from the 1984 movie Purple Rain. The song was never released as a single and had no standalone music video.

pops.text: This is track four on Purple Rain, released June 25, 1984 — Prince's sixth album and the soundtrack to his film debut.
It was never a single and never got a music video; its screen life is this performance scene in the Purple Rain film.
The opening dialogue — 'Wendy?' 'Yes, Lisa?' — is Revolution members Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman, who co-wrote the song.
The writing credits are unusually wide: Prince shares them with Melvoin, Coleman, keyboardist Dr. Fink, and his own father, John L. Nelson.
Nelson's contribution is real: the elegiac piano section, known as 'Father's Song,' was composed by Prince's father, a jazz pianist.
The album version is an edit. Prince's original cut ran several minutes longer as an extended suite.
That full-length 'hallway speech' version finally saw release in 2017 on the Purple Rain Deluxe expanded edition.
In the film, the Revolution perform it at Minneapolis's First Avenue club while rival Morris Day looks on.
The lyric casts love as a malfunctioning machine — Prince hunting for 'the righteous one' while the computer runs blue.
Purple Rain the album spent 24 consecutive weeks at #1 on the Billboard 200 — this deep cut sat at the heart of it.

title: Who's Gonna Ride Your Wild Horses
description: Achtung Baby's aching fifth track, presented in its official Zoo TV-era video — the final single from the album, built around the Edge's distorted guitar storm and Bono's plea to a dangerous lover.

pops.text: This is the fifth track on Achtung Baby (1991), U2's reinvention album recorded in Berlin and Dublin.
It began as a demo at STS Studios in Dublin in 1990, before the Berlin sessions reshaped the band's sound.
Producers were Steve Lillywhite with Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois — Lillywhite was brought in to finish several tracks, including this one.
Jimmy Iovine famously preferred the rough demo version when Bono played it to him.
It was released as the album's fifth and final single on November 23, 1992.
The single charted at #14 in the UK and #35 in the US, and reached #2 on the US rock chart.
The single featured the Temple Bar Remix — a strings-and-piano version many in the band's camp preferred to the album mix.
Its B-sides were covers: the Rolling Stones' 'Paint It Black' and Creedence Clearwater Revival's 'Fortunate Son.'
The single sleeve is Anton Corbijn's photo of Bono in a Trabant; line up the four Achtung Baby single covers and they form one picture of the band with the car.
The single also included Bono's solo recording of 'Can't Help Falling in Love,' cut for the film Honeymoon in Vegas.

title: Owner Of A Lonely Heart
description: Yes' prog-to-pop reinvention in Storm Thorgerson's surreal official video, filmed in London: actor Danny Webb plays a man seized for interrogation who escapes to a rooftop and leaps off, transforming into a bird of prey. The Trevor Horn-produced lead single from 90125 became the band's only US #1.

pops.text: This is the opening track and lead single of 90125, released on 24 October 1983, a few weeks ahead of the album.
Trevor Rabin originated the song in 1979 — by his account he wrote the whole thing while going to the toilet, then demoed it on a four-track tape machine at home.
The band behind it was not called Yes at first: Rabin, Chris Squire and Alan White formed a new group named Cinema, which only became Yes when singer Jon Anderson rejoined in April 1983.

Producer Trevor Horn — himself a former Yes singer, on 1980's Drama — recognised the demo's 'snap jump cut' intro and chorus as a hit, but spent about seven months persuading Rabin to rewrite the verse lyrics.

Its famous stabs and break use a five-second sample of Funk, Inc.'s 'Kool Is Back,' loaded into Horn's Fairlight CMI and played by drummer Alan White — Questlove has cited it as the first use of a sample as a breakbeat.

Chris Squire replaced Rabin's original bridge with a Motown-influenced section, and played his bass part on a custom Electra MPC Outlaw through a 100-watt Marshall amp, using its built-in octave drop for that sub-bass weight.

Anderson rewrote the second verse, including the line 'Watch it now, the eagle in the sky' — so Horn and engineer Gary Langan cheekily added a gunshot sound effect right after it, 'shooting down' the eagle.
The video was directed by Storm Thorgerson of Hipgnosis, who had already designed Yes album covers — Going for the One and Tormato — before this clip went into heavy MTV rotation.

Keyboardist Tony Kaye is missing from the video: Eddie Jobson was standing in at the shoot, appears only in a few quick shots, and was edited out as much as possible before Kaye returned to the lineup.
It topped the Billboard Hot 100 on January 21, 1984 and held #1 for two weeks — still Yes's only US #1 single — and finished at #8 on Billboard's 1984 year-end chart.

title: Maneater
description: Hall & Oates' biggest hit in its official video — a sleek, panther-haunted performance clip for the song Daryl Hall insists was never really about a woman at all.

pops.text: This was the lead single from H2O (1982) and became the biggest hit of Hall & Oates' career.
It reached #1 on the Billboard Hot 100 on December 18, 1982, and stayed there four weeks — the longest run of their six #1 singles.
It was written by Daryl Hall, John Oates and Sara Allen, the duo's longtime lyric collaborator and Hall's partner.
Here's the twist: Hall has said the song is not about a woman — it's about New York City in the 1980s, and greed that 'will chew you up.'
Oates first worked it up as a reggae song with Edgar Winter; Hall heard it and rebuilt it around a Motown-style groove.
That slinky saxophone solo is by Charles 'Mr. Casual' DeChant, the duo's longtime saxophonist and keyboard player.
The video features an actual black panther — Oates recalled it cost a fortune, appeared for seconds, then escaped into the studio rafters, 50 feet up.
H2O peaked at #3 on the album chart but stayed on it for 68 weeks, producing three Top 10 singles.
In the UK the single reached #6, one of the duo's biggest British hits.
Hall & Oates became the most successful duo in American chart history — and this, their signature song, is a city disguised as a femme fatale.
